Inviscid · the medium reacts · 2026-09-02

The Wave That Holds

Every wave measured in this medium so far has been linear: the kick's scalar fold wave, the shove and stir's polarized waves. In a linear medium waves pass through each other and add — that is gated at 10⁻¹⁶ — and they spread, always. A soliton is the opposite: a wave whose own nonlinearity holds it together against spreading, and which survives colliding with another one. Asking whether this medium has one means asking what its nonlinearity is.

It has a specific and unusual answer. The cell's lattice constant L(a) is stationary at the working fold — dL/da = 0 at a = −30° — which is why a fold impulse decouples from everything else at linear order. Push past linear order and that same fact says the leading coupling is quadratic: folding either way shrinks the lattice by ½L″δ². So the medium's nonlinearity is not an add-on; it is the second-order remainder of the geometry that made the fold law clean. Two consequences, both exact, both measured below: a plane longitudinal wave is exactly harmonic at every amplitude and can never steepen, so all the nonlinearity there is belongs to the fold; and the fold's own on-site potential is exactly quartic, with no quadratic and no cubic term.

And yes — the medium carries a soliton. Not a KdV pulse but an envelope soliton: a fold wavepacket whose amplitude and width stand in a fixed ratio, which crosses hundreds of cells without spreading while the identical packet in the harmonic model melts.

A · w = 48  ·  ω(q) = sin(q/2)  ·  Von-site = 4δ⁴  ·  a plane shove: exactly harmonic

plane-symmetric bulk · exact soft-joint dynamics · no linearisation

What is being integrated

A plane-symmetric state of the bulk medium — one that depends only on position along one axis — reduces exactly to one cell per plane with three bonds: one to the next plane, and two tying the cell to its own transverse neighbours. Of that cell's seven coordinates only two ever move. Starting from any state where the cells are unrotated and displaced only along the axis, the full seven-coordinate force has no torque and no transverse component, to 10⁻¹⁶, so the coordinates the reduction drops can never be excited. The medium's plane waves are exactly a two-field lattice: a longitudinal displacement and a fold angle, one of each per plane.

Those two fields turn out to be the same harmonic chain — on-site 4, coupling −2, mass 8 apiece, so both have ω = sin(q/2) exactly, both travel at ½, and the two branches are exactly degenerate. That degeneracy is the one the polarized lane reports as the longitudinal branch sitting on top of the fold at ½; here it is in closed form. Everything below is the same energy the model uses everywhere else — the true separation of every joint, not a linearisation of it — integrated with the cell's real, fold-dependent inertia.

Height against distance travelled

Envelope height as each packet crosses the lattice, exact (copper) against harmonic (slate). The soliton keeps — of its launch height over — lattice steps while the harmonic packet falls to — and more than doubles its width. Both travel at the same group velocity: the nonlinearity changes the packet's shape, not its speed.

The family: amplitude × width

Solitons come in a one-parameter family with A · w = 48 — taller means narrower, in exact inverse proportion. Three members an octave apart in amplitude, each launched at its predicted width, each holding its height. That inverse law is the signature of a focusing envelope equation, and it is a prediction the medium was not fitted to.

the test that separates a soliton from a solitary wave

And it survives a collision

A lump that merely holds together is a solitary wave. A soliton is one that can hit another and come out unchanged. Two of these packets are launched at each other head-on. They pass through, and on the far side both have their heights and widths back — but they are not where free propagation would have left them. That displacement is the collision's only trace, and it is the thing a linear medium cannot produce: in the harmonic control the two packets superpose exactly, pass through with zero shift, and emerge already spreading. Switch between the two above.

Measured, on a longer ring than the gate's: each packet comes back at 6.09° and 6.13° against the 6.00° they were launched at — full height, within the breathing the lattice soliton does anyway — and each is displaced 0.90 planes forward along its own direction of travel. Run the identical experiment in the harmonic model and the shift is 0.000: the two packets superpose exactly, which is the same fact the kick lane gates at 10⁻¹⁶, and they arrive at the far side already down to 61% of their launch height. The shift is the collision's signature, and only the nonlinear medium has one.

Why an envelope soliton and not a KdV pulse. At long wavelength the fold and longitudinal branches are not merely degenerate, they are phase-matched: a fold pulse's amplitude-squared source travels at exactly the speed of the strain wave it drives, so the transfer never dephases and a broad fold pulse pumps itself into a strain wave instead of holding together — measured, a 2° pulse of width 16 loses half its height by t = 200 and turns bipolar. Give the packet a carrier instead and that second-harmonic resonance detunes as q³. What remains is the hard quartic against the band's own curvature: focusing, and a bright envelope soliton. The medium carries the soliton it can hold, and refuses the other one.

Scope. Exact kinematics and the exact soft-joint energy, no linearisation anywhere; the restriction is to plane-symmetric states, which is a uniaxial plane wave in the bulk. Fold excursions stay well inside the physical ±60° window. The collision is measured to be nearly elastic and the radiation is quantified — this lattice is not integrable and no row here claims it is. The fold lane is The Kick; the polarized lane is Polarized; closure is the doubled block per Decision 22.
